messages.body_plain:
On 5/1/13 6:07 PM, rubi wrote:

> I'm following up on an old conversation you posted on the development mailing list, regarding saving log likelihoods for
> WAIC.
>
>  From your post I understand that ll_y should save the log-likelihoods for each data point for each sample:
>
> generated quantities {
>       double ll_y[N,T];
>
>       for (n in 1:N)
>         for (t in 1:T)
>           ll_y[N,T] <- normal_log(alpha[n] + beta[n] * (x[t] - xbar),sigma_y);
>     }
>
> Shouldn't it be:
>
> ll_y[n,t] <- normal_log(alpha[n] + beta[n] * (x[t] - xbar),sigma_y);
>
> instead of:
>
> ll_y[N,T] <- normal_log(alpha[n] + beta[n] * (x[t] - xbar),sigma_y);

Absolutely.  The former will only set one entry.
Sorry for the buggy example.

You want to look at the formulas for computed p_{WAIC 1}
and "computed p_{WAIC 2}" in the paper Andrew linked (by
Andrew, Jessica Hwang and Aki Vehtari):

http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/waic_understand_final.pdf

Note that unlike DIC, you don't need to evaluate the log
probability at the posterior mean.  But you still can't
evaluate the formula fully within Stan, because you need
averages across samples.  But it should be pretty easy in R.

Note that Andrew has a habit of renaming things.  "WAIC" was
called the "widely applicable information criteria" by
Watanabe.

If you get an example working, it'd be great if you could post
it back to the list.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: sort [for mixture components]
messages.body_plain:
On 5/1/13 7:42 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> B
> Do we have a sort() function or something similar in Stan?

No.  There's an index of functions in the very back of
the manual.

It is on the to-do list of functions to add :-)

>  I'm fitting a mixture model and thought it would be convenient to parameterize based
 > on the ordering of the modes (i.e., redefining so that mu[1]<mu[2]<mu[3] etc).
 > I know I could do this using a series of contstraints but I thought it would
 > easier via sorting?

All you need is the ordered type, where

    ordered[K] mu;

declares mu to be a vector in increasing order, which means

    mu[1] <= mu[2] <= ... <= mu[K].

I haven't tried using it to identify a mixture model.
But now that I think about it, it may be better than
sorting because if the true values are

    mu[1] = 0.5    sigma[1] = 1.5
    mu[2] = 0.55   sigma[2] = 0.25
    ...

then you might find the first two mixture components changing
order in a posterior based on sorting, which would definitely mess
up R-hat.

 > I was playing around with the mixture model in the
 > Stan manual and I realized that its results are not so easily interpretable
 > because any mixture component could correspond to any of the modes.

This has already come up several times on the users' list.

If you sort it out with ordering and it works, I'll revise the
section of the manual for the next release.

- Bob

That could certainly blow out memory.  Just
the double values in a 5600 x 5600 matrix take up
250MB.  If they're auto-dif vars, it's around triple
that.  (We could cut this down with a good symmetric
matrix implementation, but we don't have one and neither
does the Eigen lib we're using.

Maybe Ben has some idea on how to reformulate this
more efficiently?

Even if you can get this model off the ground, it's
going to be slow.  It'll require on the order of
O(N^3) operations to run solvers on it, which is
on the order of 2e+11.   And that'll be per leapfrog
step per iteration.

- Bob

There's a section on sorting and interpolation.
But you're right --- sort() itself isn't on the list!

Issue 1 is which types it'll work for.  Probably
just

    real[]
    int[]
    vector
    row_vector

We would not want it to sort in place.  So you'd have
to copy to a std::vector, apply std::sort, then return
(for real[] and int[]) or use to map an Eigen vector (for
vector and row_vector).

The to-do list did have this:

   -- rank(v,s): number of components of v less than v[s]
   -- ranked(v,s): s-th smallest component of v

These are BUGS functions.

http://www.mrc-bsu.cam.ac.uk/bugs/winbugs/manual14.pdf

The first can be implemented
in constant memory and O(s) time.  The second can be
implemented in O(s) memory and O(n log min(s,n-s)) time.

With sort(), I don't think we'd need these functions.
See this discussion on the JAGS list (JAGS uses sort()
instead of rank() and ranked()):

http://sourceforge.net/p/mcmc-jags/discussion/610037/thread/64ce3a9c

- Bob

Hi Bob,

I programmed the MVCAR in STAN because the OpenBUGS MVCAR implementation only accepts a Wishart as prior for the scale matrix. The required variance-of-one constraint in the model demands a unit (or at least a constant) diagonal. And STAN has this really great (positive-definitive) correlation matrix with unit-diagonal and flat priors on the off-diagonal elements. Hence if you or Ben have an idea how to get the model of the ground that would be absolutely great!

Best,
Marcel

messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, May 2, 2013 3:32:58 AM UTC-4, Marcel Jonker wrote:
> I programmed the MVCAR in STAN because the OpenBUGS MVCAR implementation only accepts a Wishart as prior for the scale matrix. The required variance-of-one constraint in the model demands a unit (or at least a constant) diagonal. And STAN has this really great (positive-definitive) correlation matrix with unit-diagonal and flat priors on the off-diagonal elements. Hence if you or Ben have an idea how to get the model of the ground that would be absolutely great!

Clarification: The prior on a correlation matrix is jointly uniform (iff the shape hyperparameter is 1.0) but not marginally uniform on the correlations.

As for using such a prior with a really large correlation matrix, doing would be more feasible if it were possible to work directly with its Cholesky factor and thus avoid some O(K^3) operations. messages.subject_clean: bug in stan with geometric series
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I am developing a model for which I need to sum up exp(-k * t) terms. This summation is done in the transformed parameters block. To speed up things I decided to represent this as geometric series. However, if you do that, then Stan does very weird things. It looks like Stan can not correctly auto-differentiate the term

1-pow(exp(-k * t), 100)/(1 - exp(-k * t))

with k being 0.05 or so and t=50. Is it possible that stan is choking on the very small number which is the result of taking the power 100 of the exponential?

Many thanks in advance!

Best,
Sebastian

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

 If there is a way to estimate the model with the current version of STAN, that would be great - even if it samples very slowly - because it's somewhat urgent by now. The problematic matrix is the Kronecker product of a 4x4 correlation matrix and a large adjacency matrix (loaded as data), so the correlation matrix itself is pretty small. Only the precision matrix of the mult_normal_prec is large. Perhaps that makes a difference?

Date: Thu, 2 May 2013 07:12:23 -0700
From: goodri...@gmail.com

To: stan-...@googlegroups.com
Subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: GeoBUGS distributions

On Thursday, May 2, 2013 3:32:58 AM UTC-4, Marcel Jonker wrote:
> I programmed the MVCAR in STAN because the OpenBUGS MVCAR implementation only accepts a Wishart as prior for the scale matrix. The required variance-of-one constraint in the model demands a unit (or at least a constant) diagonal. And STAN has this really great (positive-definitive) correlation matrix with unit-diagonal and flat priors on the off-diagonal elements. Hence if you or Ben have an idea how to get the model of the ground that would be absolutely great!

Clarification: The prior on a correlation matrix is jointly uniform (iff the shape hyperparameter is 1.0) but not marginally uniform on the correlations.

As for using such a prior with a really large correlation matrix, doing would be more feasible if it were possible to work directly with its Cholesky factor and thus avoid some O(K^3) operations. It is technically possible to do so with Stan syntax but if it isn't urgent, it would probably be better to wait until we can make Cholesky factors be primitive types.

Ben

On Thursday, May 2, 2013 12:52:18 PM UTC-4, Marcel Jonker wrote:
>  If there is a way to estimate the model with the current version of STAN, that would be great - even if it samples very slowly - because it's somewhat urgent by now. The problematic matrix is the Kronecker product of a 4x4 correlation matrix and a large adjacency matrix (loaded as data), so the correlation matrix itself is pretty small. Only the precision matrix of the mult_normal_prec is large. Perhaps that makes a difference?

It wouldn't help much, in part because the correlation matrix is small and in part because even if you had the Cholesky factor, our matrix multiplication operations generally wouldn't exploit the fact that it is triangular.

If you have something like

Sigma^-1 = (D - a * W) %x% Lambda

where Lambda is a correlation matrix and are going to multiply that from both sides by a vector y and D - a * W is sparse, then you can be more efficient without explicitly constructing the Kronecker product. Basically, make an array of 4-vectors that holds the product of Lambda post-multiplied by each 4-element segment of y. Scale those by the appropriate (if non-zero) element of D - a * W, sum up to get a single vector, premultiply that by transpose(y), multiply that sum by 0.5 and subtract it from lp__.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
I have a very simple working example of computing WAIC from Stan samples. I did it entirely in R, though, to avoid having to store all those likelihoods in the Stan output. I'll go ahead and attach the script, in case it dispels some confusion for someone. (The script is very didactic, using loops and redundancy to make the algorithm more transparent. It could definitely be refactored for speed.)

The formula I used is the p_{WAIC 2} on page 8 of Gelman, Hwang, & Vehtari.

I also have an experimental module for glmer2stan that computes WAIC. I haven't put it up on github yet, as I'm not sure I understand WAIC yet, and also I'm not sure how to deal with WAIC in zero-inflated models. But this functionality will appear before long. The strategy I've taken, again, is to do everything outside of Stan, saving on storage. I have some Stan models with 20k parameters and 14k data points, and I doubt saving the likelihoods in Stan is going to be a sane approach there.

>        sadn <- exp(log_sum_exp(0, -ka * nd * TAU)) - 2;
>        sadf <- exp(log(-1*sadn) - log(-1*sad));

Here are some more helpful functions:

    log1p_exp(u) =def= log_sum_exp(0, u)

Also note that log(-1 * v) == log(-v).

How do you guarantee that sadn < -0 and sad < 0 so
that the log works in the definition of sadf?  See
the comment down at the bottom.

The -2 is going to be problematic anyway, as it
forces you out of the log scale.

Here's a general post about how and why to use log_sum_exp:

https://hips.seas.harvard.edu/blog/2013/01/09/computing-log-sum-exp/

> Very ugly, but it seems to work.
> If someone is aware of more elegant solution, I would appreciate it.

I'm afraid there's really no way around it for these
kinds of operations.  Even if you change the scale of
the data or parameters, it's still better to use log_sum_exp.
We build a lot of this kind of thing into the distributions
(such as using a poisson_log(x) instead of poisson(exp(x))).
And we're always looking for suggestions to make it better.

But if you do your own arithmetic, you can still run into
arithmetic problems.

 > It looks to me I
> am experiencing numerical instabilities.

Almost certainly numerical issues given the scale of the numbers
and operations you're using.

> Are there any guidelines around for what are good and bad practice expressions
> in the context of autdiff stuff?

It's not autodiff per se, but just basic floating point
arithmetic.  Which can be very subtle and which I'm still
coming to grips with.

The guidelines for Stan are basically the same as for any
other numerical software.  Unfortunately, there are a huge
number of guidelines --- whole books just introducing
the numerical subtleties of basic arithmetic, then more
books on matrix algebra, whole papers on special functions
like gamma, etc. etc. etc.  Ben knows the most about the
matrix algebra issues, but none of us are numerical analysts.

Tip 1.  Always work on the log scale if you can to prevent
overflow and underflow that would arise on the natural scale.
For example, don't take the product of a bunch of probabilities,
take the sum of the logs.

Tip 2.  Avoid catastrophic cancellation in subtraction

You can put tip 1 and tip 2 together and use

    log1m(x) =def= log(1 - x)

Autodiff is rarely the problem if the operators and
themselves don't have arithmetic problems.  Autodiff just
involves the evaluation of analytic derivatives by
tracing through the program.

For instance, if you have exp(x), then the derivative
is exp(x), and both have exactly the same stability issues
(x < -700 or so underflows; x > 700 or so overflows).
If the expression is log(x), the derivative is 1/x.
1/x produces extreme values if x is extreme.

One extra subtlety for us is that there are implicit
exponentiations in places.  For instance, if you declare
a variable positive (lower=0) then there's an implicit exp()
applied to map the unconstrained parameter back to the
positive numbers.

> However, once I done this I run into another bizarre problem:
>
> Error : No acceptably small step size could be found. Perhaps the posterior is not continuous?
> error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done
>
> I know that I handle very small quantities in my problem - does it mean I have to switch to log scale on all my
> computations? Or can I force Stan to use a certain lower step size?

You can initialize the step size or just set it outright.
But this error message means no step size is small enough to move
from the current parameter value to another parameter value in
support.  This usually happens if you initialize somewhere outisde
of the support of the log probability function.  For instance, if one of your
sad or sadn isn't negative.

It can also come up if you're very close to a constraint boundary,
like positive definiteness for covariance matrices.

You might want to try the dump of derivatives if the problem's
not too large (it uses finite differences, which can be slow in
large dimensions).  If the log probability is NaN or -infinity,
the initialization point is out of support.  (Be
warned --- the dump is on the unconstrained scale.)

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi Marcel,

I've been working on something related to this and I realized that
perhaps the easiest way to do what you need in Stan in a reasonably
efficient way is to implement a matrix_normal(_prec) distribution.  I
believe the distribution you're computing can formulated in terms of a
matrix normal distribution, see
http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_normal_distribution for details.

If this is the case let me know and I should be able to get a fairly
efficient version of that in Stan pretty quickly.

Cheers,
Marcus

>>> mult_normal_prec is large. Perhaps that makes a difference?
>>
>>
>> It wouldn't help much, in part because the correlation matrix is small and
>> in part because even if you had the Cholesky factor, our matrix
>> multiplication operations generally wouldn't exploit the fact that it is
>> triangular.
>>
>> If you have something like
>>
>> Sigma^-1 = (D - a * W) %x% Lambda
>>
>> where Lambda is a correlation matrix and are going to multiply that from
>> both sides by a vector y and D - a * W is sparse, then you can be more
>> efficient without explicitly constructing the Kronecker product. Basically,
>> make an array of 4-vectors that holds the product of Lambda post-multiplied
>> by each 4-element segment of y. Scale those by the appropriate (if non-zero)
>> element of D - a * W, sum up to get a single vector, premultiply that by
>> transpose(y), multiply that sum by 0.5 and subtract it from lp__.
>
>
> Attached is an R script that demonstrates this idea of circumventing the
> Kronecker product, which could be adapted to Stan syntax fairly easily but
> it would probably be worth the effort to avoid multiplying by elements of D
> - a * W that are zero.
>
> Ben

There aren't any issues with log1m(x) of which we're
aware --- if x > 1, we'll throw an exception, but RStan
should be trapping that if you're running in "debug" mode.
One thing you might try is printing the x before calling
log1m to see if that's what's happening.  You can even
say something like

   if (x > 1) print("bad x for log1m(x), x=", x);

Are you using set_cppo("debug")?  If so, and RStan
is still crashing, that's a bug in RStan, and we'd
really appreciate it if you could send us the full model
and data (or even better, a smaller model where we
can reproduce the error).

Jiqiang/Ben:  what's the default mode with RStan?

I think what makes most sense is to have two modes:

   standard: -O3, check bounds, never crashes R (i.e., trap all exceptions)

   fast:     -O3, no bounds checks, may crash R

When somebody sets "fast" mode we should indicate that
(a) how much faster they can expect things to go, and (b) that
they're running the risk of crashing R and losing their
environment.

It may also make sense to have a third option if there's
some reason to ever compile with -O0:

   debug:   -O0, +debug, check bounds, trap all exceptions

The problem with that is that we can't compile with -O0 in
Windows -- it blows out the gcc's memory.

- Bob

I think you have to do both -O0 and -g or add -mtune=native or something. Last I checked -O0 alone would work. In any event, I don't think there is gdb for Windows so it is not as if they can debug it, and debug mode is useful for !Windows with gdb or lldb.

Ben

> >> I have a very simple working example of computing WAIC from Stan samples. I did it entirely in R, though, to avoid

> >> confusion for someone. (The script is very didactic, using loops and redundancy to make the algorithm more
> >> transparent. It could definitely be refactored for speed.)
> >>
> >> The formula I used is the p_{WAIC 2} on page 8 of Gelman, Hwang, & Vehtari.
> >>
> >> I also have an experimental module for glmer2stan that computes WAIC. I haven't put it up on github yet, as I'm not
> >> sure I understand WAIC yet, and also I'm not sure how to deal with WAIC in zero-inflated models. But this
> >> functionality will appear before long. The strategy I've taken, again, is to do everything outside of Stan, saving on

Hi!

Finally...problem solved! To summarize: My equations rely on certain parameters being smaller than 0 otherwise bad things happen. Now, I did enforce this correctly for the group parameter, but individual subjects were allowed to violate these constrains. Once I realized this and fixed it, my model just runs fine!

Concerning the memory issues I encountered: I checked the code and saw quite a number of new operators in the stan::agrad::log1p functions. I think what happened is that I triggered with a x>1 in log1m an exception which caused the normal program flow to be aborted and ultimately some things did go wrong in this case with memory management. But I am only guessing here. BTW, is it really necessary to program stuff with pointers and new operators? I learned many times to stay away from these things...

Thanks for your support!

Best,

Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] WAIC's a go
messages.body_plain:
The downside of computing the per-data-point likelihoods
in either Stan's generated quantities block or in R is
that you have to duplicate information that's in the model.
The problem in general with doing this in R is that I don't think
all of the parameterizations of distributions match.  (We should
really have a table for this in our doc.)

What we'd really like to do, but haven't quite figured out how to do,
is do all of this automatically based on the model specification.
What I envision is something like this in a very very simple case:

model {
   prior {
     mu ~ normal(0,10);
     sigma ~ uniform(0,100);
   }
   likelihood {

     for (n in 1:N)

       y[n] ~ normal(mu,sigma);  // save these quantities
   }
}

so that we could figure out the likelihoods here.
Then we could potentially monitor these as we go and
calculate running totals using something like Welford's
algorithm.

The reason this isn't so easy is that Stan allows all
kinds of things other than simple sampling statements in
the code.  In general, the likelihood might require side
calculations, local variables, etc. which are hard to tease
apart from the relevant amounts.

The alternative that Andrew's been suggesting would be
to somehow annotate the regular code, so it'd look more
like:

model {
   mu ~ normal(0,10);
   sigma ~ uniform(0,100);

   for (n in 1:N)

     y[n] ~ normal(mu,sigma);  @likelihood
}

where the annotation @likelihood indicates that
the likelihood for a variableis being defined.  Another
way of doing this would be something like this:

model {
   ...
   for (n in 1:N) {
     real ll;
     for (n in 1:N) {
       ll <- normal_log(y[n],mu,sigma);
       for_waic(y[n],ll); // store likelihood for WAIC
       lp__ <- lp__ + ll;
     }
   }

Any of these approaches bring up all kinds of issues
where things can go wrong.  For instance, if there's an
if/else statement, you have to make sure each variable gets
its likelihood in every block.

- Bob

On 5/5/13 2:07 PM, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> Hi!
>
> I will do the backtrace and post it. Concerning pointers: Why not use shared_ptr or unique_ptr c++ facilities?
> Performance reasons? These are usually much safer to use - at least I came to this conclusion for my own programming.

Yes, performance.  We use an arena-based memory management
strategy where we allocate blocks of memory, use them for auto-dif,
then free them all at once.

You can think of what we're doing as implementing something
like the shared_ptr or unique_ptr in that we use a pointer
to implementation (PIMPL) idiom for the client code (stan::agrad::var).
You see the same kind of pointer/memory abstraction underlying
std::vector and Eigen::Matrix.

We've specialized operator new for our vari classes for
reverse-mode auto-dif.  Then we free the memory all at once
after a gradient calculation.

The bug that's in there now, I believe, is that we're
not properly freeing memory related to a gradient calc when
we hit an exception.  So we don't have a strict
resource allocation is initialization (RIAA) pattern for
our client code, which is very dangerous.

- Bob

messages.subject: RE: [stan-users] Re: GeoBUGS distributions
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

Ben has been so kind to explain where the relationship between F ~ multi_normal_prec(zeros, prec_matrix) and his previously posted multiplication of y' * prec_matrix * y comes from. For those interested (I thought it was pretty cool), I attached it here.

Let Sigma_inv be the precision matrix defined by Kronecker_product( D - a*W , corr_matrix ). Then, F ~ multi_normal_prec(zeros, Sigma_inv) is (after taking the logarithm) proportional to (see http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multivariate_normal_distribution#Density_function )
log(det(Sigma_inv)) - 0.5 * (y - zeros)' * Sigma_inv * (y - zeros)

or since the vector of zeros is irrelevant
log(det(Sigma_inv)) - 0.5 * y' * Sigma_inv * y

So, it is worth looking into optimized ways to calculate y' * Sigma_inv * y where you don't have to explicitly form the big, sparse Sigma_inv matrix via Kronecker_product( D - a*W , corr_matrix ).
I neglected to mention the part about log(det(Sigma_inv)) but again you would want to exploit the properties of the Kronecker product (see http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kronecker_product#Properties ) and write

log(det(Sigma_inv))

as

p * log(det(D - a*W)) + n * log(det(corr_matrix))

where p and n are the order of the respective matrices.

All together, instead of doing

F ~ multi_normal_prec( zeros, Kronecker_product( D - a*W , corr_matrix ) );

do the equivalent two steps

lp__ <- lp__ + p * log_determinant(DmaW) + n * log_determinant(corr_matrix); // determinant part
lp__ <- lp__ - 0.5 * that_trick_I_posted; // kernel part

It may be possible to speed this up further. For example, instead of doing log(det(corr_matrix)), I think it would be faster to take the Cholesky factor of corr_matrix and calculate twice the sum of the log diagonal elements, but for a 4x4 matrix, it probably won't make much difference. Another thing is to not literally compute D - a * W but instead exploit the fact that the elements of W are either 0 or 1 and do

matrix[p,p] DmaW;
for(i in 1:p) {
  DmaW[i,i] <- diagD[i]; // i'th diagonal element
  for(j in 1:p) if(W[i,j] ==1) DmaW[i,j] <- -a; // off-diagonals
}

Again, it may be faster to take the Cholesky factor of DmaW and use that to calculate the log determinant than to do log(det(DmaW)), which uses a QR factorization.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
What you want is

model {
   loglam ~ multi_normal(mu,Sigma);
   Y ~ poisson(exp(loglam));
}

You may also need to define Y, mu and loglam as column vectors instead
of row vectors.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
Ok, my apologies, I didn't look closely enough at your model.  You
actually need to define loglam and mu differently.  One way to do it
is to use the following definitions:

matrix[2,n] loglam;

matrix[2,n] mu;

and with model block:

model {
  for (i in 1:n) {

    col(loglam,i) ~ multi_normal(col(mu,i),Sigma);
    Y[i] ~ poisson(exp(col(loglam,i)));
  }
}

Where the col() function extracts a column of the matrix.

Hopefully that helps, and sorry for the confusion.

Cheers,
Marcus

Re: [stan-users] Re: How to vectorize pow()
messages.body_plain:
As Ben said, it's unlikely that the pow() calls are the slow parts of
this model.  Why do you think it's that line that is slowing things
down?

I assume that N is fairly large, in which case you might be able to
speed up this line:

y ~ multi_normal(muvec, diag_matrix(thesd)*meascorr*diag_matrix(thesd));

by dividing y and muvec by thesd.

(y./thesd) ~ mult_normal(muvec./thesd,meascorr);

If thesd was a parameter, you'd also need to do a correction to lp__:

lp__ <- lp__ - sum(log(thesd))

but since thesd is data, this would just be a constant and is unnecessary.

Hope this helps a bit.

Cheers,
Marcus

>> vectorize the power function, or some other way around this.

>
> There isn't a version of the pow() function that accepts a vector, so what
> you have there is basically the way to do it. It might be slightly faster if

> Ben

As the message indicates, this is only an issue if you see a lot of
them and the sampler isn't able to move.  If you want to get rid of
this you can tweak the bounds on tau to avoid a nearly singular Sigma.
 Specifically,

 real<lower=(-1 + 1e-8),upper=(1 - 1e-8)> tau;

So tau can never quite get to 1 or -1.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
Of course!
I used
real<lower=-0.99,upper=0.99> tau;
which solved the issue.

Cheers,

Peter

On Tue, May 7, 2013 at 12:48 PM, Marcus Brubaker

<marcus.a...@gmail.com> wrote:
> As the message indicates, this is only an issue if you see a lot of
> them and the sampler isn't able to move.  If you want to get rid of
> this you can tweak the bounds on tau to avoid a nearly singular Sigma.
>  Specifically,
>
>  real<lower=(-1 + 1e-8),upper=(1 - 1e-8)> tau;
>
> So tau can never quite get to 1 or -1.
>
> Cheers,
> Marcus
>
>
>
> On Tue, May 7, 2013 at 2:41 PM, Peter Solymos <sol...@ualberta.ca> wrote:
>> Thanks Marcus, that did the trick, but note I had to swap indices in loglam:
>>
>> model {
>>     for (i in 1:n) {
>>         col(loglam,i) ~ multi_normal(col(mu,i),Sigma);
>>         Y1[i] ~ poisson_log(loglam[1,i]);
>>         Y2[i] ~ poisson_log(loglam[2,i]);
>>     }
>>     tau ~ uniform(-1, 1);
>> }
>>
>> Now adaptation complains about Sigma not being positive definite, but
>> as far as I read on the list, this can be quite safely ignored:
>>
>> "
>> Informational Message: The parameter state is about to be Metropolis
>> rejected due to the following underlying, non-fatal (really) issue
>> (and please ignore that what comes next might say 'error'): Invalid
>> value of Sigma: Error in function validate transformed params d: Sigma
>> is not positive definite. Sigma(0,0) is 0.25.
>> If the problem persists across multiple draws, you might have a
>> problem with an initial state or a gradient somewhere.
>>  If the problem does not persist, the resulting samples will still be
>> drawn from the posterior.
>> "
>>
>> Thanks for your help!
>>
>> Peter
>>
>>
>>

Thanks Ben,
It's all good now. I post the current version below that works without
any errors/warnings/notes.
Cheers,
Peter

--

library(MASS)
set.seed(1234)
n <- 100
beta1 <- c(1, -1)
beta2 <- c(0.5, 0.5)
sigma1 <- 0.5
sigma2 <- 0.8
tau12 <- 0.5
x <- runif(n)
X <- model.matrix(~x)
mu1 <- drop(X %*% beta1)
mu2 <- drop(X %*% beta2)
Sig <- diag(c(sigma1, sigma2)^2)
Sig[2,1] <- Sig[1,2] <- sigma1*sigma2*tau12
ee <- mvrnorm(n, c(0,0), Sig)
Y1 <- rpois(n, exp(mu1 + ee[,1]))
Y2 <- rpois(n, exp(mu2 + ee[,2]))

joint_PLn <- '
data {
    int<lower=0> n;
    int<lower=0> Y1[n];
    int<lower=0> Y2[n];
    matrix[2,n] mu;
    real<lower=0> sigma1;
    real<lower=0> sigma2;
}
parameters {

    real<lower=-0.99,upper=0.99> tau;

    matrix[2,n] loglam;
}
transformed parameters {
    cov_matrix[2] Sigma;
    Sigma[1,1] <- sigma1*sigma1;
    Sigma[2,2] <- sigma2*sigma2;
    Sigma[1,2] <- sigma1*sigma2*tau;
    Sigma[2,1] <- sigma1*sigma2*tau;
}
model {
    for (i in 1:n) {
        col(loglam,i) ~ multi_normal(col(mu,i),Sigma);

        Y1[i] ~ poisson_log(loglam[1,i]);

        Y2[i] ~ poisson_log(loglam[2,i]);

    }
    tau ~ uniform(-1, 1);
}
'
dat <- list(n = n, mu=rbind(mu1,mu2), Y1=Y1, Y2=Y2,

    sigma1=sigma1, sigma2=sigma2)

f <- stan(model_code=joint_PLn, data=dat)

>
> Ben has been so kind to explain where the relationship between F ~ multi_normal_prec(zeros, prec_matrix) and his previously posted multiplication of y' * prec_matrix * y comes from. For those interested (I thought it was pretty cool), I attached it here.

>
> Let Sigma_inv be the precision matrix defined by Kronecker_product( D - a*W , corr_matrix ). Then, F ~ multi_normal_prec(zeros, Sigma_inv) is (after taking the logarithm) proportional to (see http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multivariate_normal_distribution#Density_function )
> log(det(Sigma_inv)) - 0.5 * (y - zeros)' * Sigma_inv * (y - zeros)
>

>

> I neglected to mention the part about log(det(Sigma_inv)) but again you would want to exploit the properties of the Kronecker product (see http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kronecker_product#Properties ) and write
>
> log(det(Sigma_inv))
>
> as
>
> p * log(det(D - a*W)) + n * log(det(corr_matrix))
>
> where p and n are the order of the respective matrices.

> All together, instead of doing

> F ~ multi_normal_prec( zeros, Kronecker_product( D - a*W , corr_matrix ) );
>
> do the equivalent two steps
>
> lp__ <- lp__ + p * log_determinant(DmaW) + n * log_determinant(corr_matrix); // determinant part
> lp__ <- lp__ - 0.5 * that_trick_I_posted; // kernel part
>
> It may be possible to speed this up further. For example, instead of doing log(det(corr_matrix)), I think it would be faster to take the Cholesky factor of corr_matrix and calculate twice the sum of the log diagonal elements, but for a 4x4 matrix, it probably won't make much difference. Another thing is to not literally compute D - a * W but instead exploit the fact that the elements of W are either 0 or 1 and do
>
> matrix[p,p] DmaW;
> for(i in 1:p) {
>   DmaW[i,i] <- diagD[i]; // i'th diagonal element
>   for(j in 1:p) if(W[i,j] ==1) DmaW[i,j] <- -a; // off-diagonals
> }
>
> Again, it may be faster to take the Cholesky factor of DmaW and use that to calculate the log determinant than to do log(det(DmaW)), which uses a QR factorization.
>
> Ben

messages.body_plain:
I added it to the to-do list.  I'd been meaning to
do something like this before.  To match log_sum_exp,
I'd want to call it something like this:

   log_diff_exp(x,y)  =def=  log(exp(x) - exp(y))

and then we can use the same rescaling track to avoid
overflow on the exp.

I'm not convinced the snippet you linked implements this
the most efficiently and arithmetically stable way possible.
Cutting out boundaries and renaming, here's that code:

   // copyright Andrew Miller, downloaded from http://snipplr.com/view/12707/
   double
   log_diff_exp(double x, double y) {
     double diff = x - y;
     diff /= 2.0;
     return (x + y) / 2.0 + log(exp(diff) - exp(-diff));
   }

Given that we know x > y, we can just do this:

    log(exp(x) - exp(y))

    = log(exp(x) * (exp(x)/exp(x) - exp(y)/exp(x)))

    = log(exp(x)) + log(1 - exp(y)/exp(x))

    = x + log(1 - exp(y - x))

    = x + log1m(exp(y-x))

Because x > y, 0 <= exp(y-x) <= 1.

Is that the right thing to do here or is it better to use
the above form from the snippet linked above?

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] benefit of using fma?
messages.body_plain:
For now, the only advantage is that it saves a bit on the
partial derivatives.  There's a bit less memory involved
and it's a bit faster.

We also have it in place on the C++ side so that we
have full coverage of the basic C++ math libs.  See:

http://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/numeric/math/fma

It should probably be recoded to call the built-in
library fma() code, which can sometimes be compiled
down to faster machine code.  fma() is technically part
of the TR1 libraries, but it doesn't look like it got
added to the main C++ distributions until C++11.

Does anyone know more about its availability?  I'd be happy
to drop in a faster version if one were available without
using C++11.  (We're trying to avoid C++11 until R supports
it, but may give that up at some point, especially if
RStudio moves over to a clang++ and C++11 basis.

- Bob

messages.subject: workaround for cut() function?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I am new to Stan, trying to convert a model from OpenBugs to Stan.
In the model I have experimental error that I want to include in the estimate, but without the "true" measurement to be estimated/optimized
(see The Bugs Book section 9.4 p202).

So in BUGS this is:

  for (i in 1:N){
    x.observed[i] ~ dnorm(x.estimate[i], tau.x[i])
    x.cut[i] <- cut(x.estimate[i])

    y.hat[i] <- a + b * x.cut[i]
    y[i] ~ dnorm(y.hat[i], tau.y)
  }

Since there is not cut() function in stan I am wondering how to to this.

Would substracting from lp__ have the same effect as the cut() function in BUGS in this case?

  for (i in 1:N){
    x_observed[i] ~ normal(x_estimate[i], sigma_x[i]);
    lp__ -= normal_log(x_observed[i], x_estimate[i], sigma_x[i]);

    y_hat[i] <- a + b * x_estimate[i]
    y[i] ~ normal( y_hat[i], sigma_y)
   }

Is this the "correct" way of doing this?

   Many Thanks,
       Stephan

But for your model, if I manually specify the initial values for the parameters, for example,

a = 0
b = -1.7
c = 0.6
d = 1.6e6
sigma = 4

Stan still cannot sample for this model (but it won't have the error you had).  I would suggest taking a good look of the data and see if the model make sense.

--
Jiqiang

messages.subject: stan implementation for dclone package
messages.body_plain:
Dear Stan List,

This is just to inform you that I started implementing stan related code for my dclone R package.

- stan.fit is the dclone compatible version of rstan:::stan that can return coda-like mcmc.list result with n.clones attribute, so that all data cloning features are available. Most of the original stan arguments are retained as part of (...), compiled code can be efficiently reused.

- stan.parfit is the parallel implementation, allowing for the use of multicore type forking and snow type clusters.

Check out the code and seeds example at: http://dcr.r-forge.r-project.org/extras/stan.fit.R

According to plan, these will be part of dclone once rstan finds its way to CRAN. Feedback is welcome!

Cheers,

Peter

their size and build-time limitations.  Because we
need to compile code at run time (models get translated
to C++ then compiled) and because we have fat dependencies

of templating in auto-dif and the matrix libs, the build
times are also too slow.  Maybe if they relax their policies
or someone figures out how to work around them.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] workaround for cut() function?
messages.body_plain:
Not having the BUGS book to hand, could you provide
a bit more of the model and indicate what's data and
what's a parameter and what the log probability function
works out to?

If you can write the log probability function down, you
can code it in Stan.  I'm not sure all the uses of cut
in BUGS correspond to a well-formed model.

In your subtraction example, everything gets cut out
and it's like

Stan lets you do something like cut for predictive inference
in the generated quantities block, but there's no way to feed
this back into sampling for other parameters.  That is, you
need to cut from some parameters all the way down the directed
model to the leaves.

Your suggestion:

 >      x_observed[i] ~ normal(x_estimate[i], sigma_x[i]);
 >      lp__ -= normal_log(x_observed[i], x_estimate[i], sigma_x[i]);
 >

won't work because that's just an inefficient way of writing
a no-op.  That is, the model will have the same probability function
with both of these lines removed.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] workaround for cut() function?
messages.body_plain:
Here is the complete model for the example:

#-------
data{
   int<lower=0> N; # number of data points
   real x_observed[N]; # experimentally observed x
   real sigma_x[N]; # experimental error for observed x
   real y[N];
}
parameters{
   real a;
   real b;
   real sigma_y[N];
   real y_hat[N];
   real x_estimate[N]; # random variable incorporating the
                       # experimental uncertainty into the model
               # this could also be just a temporary variable
}

model{

  for (i in 1:N){
    x_observed[i] ~ normal(x_estimate[i], sigma_x[i]);
    lp__ -= normal_log(x_observed[i], x_estimate[i], sigma_x[i]);

    y_hat[i] <- a + b * x_estimate[i]
    y[i] ~ normal( y_hat[i], sigma_y)
   }
}

#--------

The experimental error x_sigma for x_observed varies a lot between data points. The idea is to use x_estimate as a random variable to sample from the distribution of x_observed during the simulation, which should be reflected in the confidence intervals for parameters a and b.
I do not want to get the x_estimate that gives me the best fit to y, I am interested how the confidence intervals for a and b change as I run multiple experiments, each experiment giving me a different set of x_observed (but there is only one set of y measurements).
The idea is to run multiple simulations with the same y but different sets of x_observable, and see which one has the tightest confidence intervals for a and b.
You mentioned that what I am doing is an inefficient way of doing a no-op, which is kinda the idea (I think), as long as x_estimate[i] is varying according to the experimental uncertainty for data point x_observed[i].

Maybe there is a better way of doing this, I am coming over from the BUGS way of doing this and trying to figure out how to do this in Stan. Any suggestions and critique are welcome.

  Many Thanks,
       S.

>
> |
> lp__ <- lp__ - whatever;
> |
>
> where whatever is the sum of the log-likelihood contributions that you don't want to influence the posterior.

In general you can indeed create the log probability
function however you want, including by substracting terms out.

Just be careful that if you write something like the original
poster suggested,

     x_observed[i] ~ normal(x_estimate[i], sigma_x[i]);

     lp__ <- lp__ - normal_log(x_observed[i], x_estimate[i], sigma_x[i]);

it's equivalent to just removing both statements, because they
exactly cancel each other out.  That's because the first statement
is just shorthand for

     lp__ <- lp__ + normal_log(x_observed[i], x_estimate[i], sigma_x[i]);

so after executing both, lp__ is back to where it started.
All the derivatives will get evaluated and will just cancel
out, too.  All of this only up to arithmetic precision, of course.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] workaround for cut() function?
messages.body_plain:
Hi.  The reason why I (and others) perceive "cut" as bad news is because when you do "cut," you are no longer doing Bayesian inference.  To put it another way, if it's really true that you don't want inference going from A to B, I don't think you want it going from B to A either.  Joint distributions go both ways.
A

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] workaround for cut() function?
messages.body_plain:
On 5/11/13 4:56 PM, sreiling wrote:
> Here is the complete model for the example:

I meant the BUGS model with the cut!

I literally meant it behaves as a no-op.
The model

> model{
>    for (i in 1:N){
>      x_observed[i] ~ normal(x_estimate[i], sigma_x[i]);
>      lp__ -= normal_log(x_observed[i], x_estimate[i], sigma_x[i]);
>
>      y_hat[i] <- a + b * x_estimate[i]
>      y[i] ~ normal( y_hat[i], sigma_y)
>     }
> }

is equivalent to the model that removes the first two statements:

 > model{
 >    for (i in 1:N){

 >      y_hat[i] <- a + b * x_estimate[i]
 >      y[i] ~ normal( y_hat[i], sigma_y)
 >     }
 > }

You do need semicolons in Stan, though, so the above won't actually compile.
You don't need to declare intermediate variables like y_hat unless you
want to see them.  Instead, you can rewrite the above model as just this:

model {
    y ~ normal(a + b * x_estimate, sigma_y);
}

It will be more efficient.

> The experimental error x_sigma for x_observed varies a lot between data points. The idea is to use x_estimate as a
> random variable to sample from the distribution of x_observed during the simulation, which should be reflected in the
> confidence intervals for parameters a and b.
> I do not want to get the x_estimate that gives me the best fit to y, I am interested how the confidence intervals for a
> and b change as I run multiple experiments, each experiment giving me a different set of x_observed (but there is only
> one set of y measurements).
> The idea is to run multiple simulations with the same y but different sets of x_observable, and see which one has the
> tightest confidence intervals for a and b.
> You mentioned that what I am doing is an inefficient way of doing a no-op, which is kinda the idea (I think), as long as
> x_estimate[i] is varying according to the experimental uncertainty for data point x_observed[i].

I'm not familiar with this approach to modeling measurement error.
I did read the linked slides and they match your description, so I
think I see what's going on.

> Maybe there is a better way of doing this, I am coming over from the BUGS way of doing this and trying to figure out how
> to do this in Stan. Any suggestions and critique are welcome.

As Andrew pointed out in another reply, if you have a joint probability,
information flows both ways just through the laws of conditional
probabilities.  All a Stan model does is specify a
joint probability p(y,theta|x) over data y, parameters theta, and covariates
(also data) x.  We then sample from p(theta|y,x).  If you can formulate the model
as a proper joint probability density, then it can probably be coded in Stan.
If not, then it definitely won't be codeable in Stan.

The only thing like the BUGS cut operator that Stan supports is
in predictive inference.  You can fit the model as you usually would,
then define predicted quantities in the generated quantities block that
can depend on the values of parameters.  This information does not flow
back into the model in a semi-supervised way.  There's an example in
the manual for HMMs where this makes a difference.

- Bob

messages.subject: Implementing NUTS in PyMC
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stan Users!

I contribute to pymc, and I'm trying to implement NUTS for pymc. I have a draft, but I am running into the problem that the variance of the samples is too high. I try to sample a normal or t distribution with stdev of 1 and I come up with a stdev of 1.07 or so (with many iterations).

So I am interested in strategies for verifying that NUTS is correctly implemented. What kinds of tests do you guys have for NUTS?

Also, do you have tips for implementing NUTS?

Cheers,
John

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Implementing NUTS in PyMC
messages.body_plain:
About the only strategy we've used is to look
at quantiles of the output and verify that they're
right using either chi-by-eye or a proper chi-square test).
You can also look at this paper of Cook, Gelman
and Rubin:

http://www.stat.cmu.edu/~acthomas/724/Cook.pdf

The NUTS algorithm itself is very subtle in its
boundary conditions.  We're in the middle of rewriting
it right now to make it more modular and comprehensible.

Sampling t-distributions is a tricky business when we're
talking about the Cauchy, because the variance isn't finite.
You might want to look at Radford Neal's slice sampling
paper for some analysis on why it's hard in general to
deal with fat tails in samplers that move in a way controlled
by energy changes broadly construed.

- Bob

messages.subject: Looping in STAN vs. looping in R (20 fold faster)
messages.subject_clean: Looping in STAN vs. looping in R (20 fold faster)
messages.body_plain:
In preparation for running a hierarchical model in STAN, we performed a timing test of two approaches. The first called STAN from R, passed a matrix of 1000x63 to STAN, looped in STAN over i=1,...,1,000 samples (rows), with each sample consisting of 63 observations from a N(mu_i=0, sigma_i=1) distribution (columns), and estimated mu_i and sigma_i. The second approach looped in R over i = 1, ...,1,000 samples and called STAN 1,000 times, once for each sample (row), passing to STAN a vector with 63 observations to estimate mu_i and sigma_i.

The second approach - looping in R - was 20 times as fast as the first approach - looping in STAN.

This is a problem because we plan to use the first approach to implement a hierarchical model on data on 16,000 samples each with 63 observations. Implementing the hierarchical model does not seem possible with the second approach. We are hoping someone can point out why our STAN code for the first approach is inefficient, and what STAN code can be used to achieve the same speed (or better) as the second approach, so that a hierarchical model can be fitted for 16,000 mu_i, sigma_i in reasonable time.

Thanks!

###########################################################################################
# Filename:  timing_20130516
# Use:  Compare timing between looping in R and STAN using simple model/data
#
# Updates:
# 20130516 DJR Initial code created
###########################################################################################

######################################################
# PACKAGES
######################################################
library(rstan)

##############################################
# Data
##############################################
set.seed(444)
mat = matrix(rnorm(63*1000,0,1),ncol=63)
r = nrow(mat)
c = ncol(mat)

######################################################
# STAN models
# stan_model1: takes in matrix, est mu/sigma for each row
# stan_model2: takes in vector, est mu/sigma for vector
######################################################

stan_model1 <- '
data {
int R; //number of rows
int C; //number of columns
  real mat[R,C]; //matrix of outcomes
}
parameters {
real mu[R]; //vector of locations
real<lower=0> sigma[R]; //vector of scales
}
model {
for (m in 1:R) {
mat[m] ~ normal(mu[m],sigma[m]);
}
}
'

stan_model2 <- '
data {
int<lower=0> C;
  real vec[C]; //vector of outcomes
}
parameters {
real mu; //location
real<lower=0> sigma; //scale
}
model {
vec ~ normal(mu,sigma);
}
'

###########################################################
# TRANSLATE AND COMPILE STAN MODEL
###########################################################
compiled1 <- stan_model(model_code = stan_model1)
compiled2 <- stan_model(model_code = stan_model2)

#####################################
# METHOD 1: Loop in Stan
#####################################

######################################################
# Assign data
######################################################
stan_data1 = list(mat = mat, R = r, C = c)
######################################################
# Run data through the model
######################################################
start = proc.time()
fit <- sampling(object=compiled1, data=stan_data1, iter=1000, chains=4, seed = 444)
time1 = proc.time() - start

#####################################
# METHOD 2: Loop in R
#####################################
start = proc.time()
for (m in 1:r) {

######################################################
# Assign data for current marker
######################################################

stan_data2 = list(vec = mat[r,], C = c)
######################################################
# Run data through the model
######################################################

fit2 <- sampling(object=compiled2, data=stan_data2, iter=1000, chains=4, seed = 444)
#################
# END FIRST LOOP
#################
}
time2 = proc.time() - start

#####################################
# Compare times between methods
#####################################

print(time1)
## Loop in Stan
##   user  system elapsed
##  191.09    3.70  196.22

print(time2)
## Loop in R
##   user  system elapsed
##  37.00    0.19   37.85

messages.body_plain:
What I had queued up to respond is below.  It expands on
my earlier comment.  I'm running the test now in another window
and will report when it's done.

On 5/16/13 2:48 PM, Steve wrote:
> In preparation for running a hierarchical model in STAN, we performed a timing test of two approaches. The first called
> STAN from R, passed a matrix of 1000x63 to STAN, looped in STAN over i=1,...,1,000 samples (rows), with each sample
> consisting of 63 observations from a N(mu_i=0, sigma_i=1) distribution (columns), and estimated mu_i and sigma_i. The
> second approach looped in R over i = 1, ...,1,000 samples and called STAN 1,000 times, once for each sample (row),
> passing to STAN a vector with 63 observations to estimate mu_i and sigma_i.
>
> The second approach - looping in R - was 20 times as fast as the first approach - looping in STAN.
>
> This is a problem because we plan to use the first approach to implement a hierarchical model on data on 16,000 samples
> each with 63 observations. Implementing the hierarchical model does not seem possible with the second approach. We are
> hoping someone can point out why our STAN code for the first approach is inefficient, and what STAN code can be used to
> achieve the same speed (or better) as the second approach, so that a hierarchical model can be fitted for 16,000 mu_i,
> sigma_i in reasonable time.

Thanks -- this is useful to know and a great example --- I'm
going to add a discussion to the optimization chapter of
the programming part.

Please let me start with a disclaimer for those who might
not read on:  we're not talking about looping
per se, which is MUCH faster in Stan than in R (because Stan
compiles down to C loops), but the issue of whether fitting a big joint
model of independent parameters is faster than fitting many individual
models.

Here's the slower joint model:

 > stan_model1 <- '
 > data {
 > int R; //number of rows
 > int C; //number of columns
 >    real mat[R,C]; //matrix of outcomes
 > }
 > parameters {
 > real mu[R]; //vector of locations
 > real<lower=0> sigma[R]; //vector of scales
 > }
 > model {
 > for (m in 1:R) {
 > mat[m] ~ normal(mu[m],sigma[m]);
 > }
 > }
 > '

The problem with the above model for speed is this
declaration:

 >    real mat[R,C]; //matrix of outcomes

coupled with this usage in the model:

 >  for (m in 1:R)
 >    mat[m] ~ normal(mu[m],sigma[m]);

There are two key issues:

1.  The call to mat[m] creates a new short-lived vector object
     which requires both a memory allocation and deallocation in every
     iteration through the loop, which is much much slower than
     arithmetic.

2.  Because mat[m] is a row vector, the copy is very inefficient
     because matrices are stored in column-major order.  If R is
     big, every element of mat[m] is going to cause a cache miss,
     which is very expensive.

Instead, I would suggest declaring mat as follows:

     row_vector[C] mat[R];

Then mat[m] just refers to an existing data structure in the
array of vectors so no copying is needed.

The reason you're seeing such a stark difference is because
this is about all this model's doing!  Every other operation in
the model is pretty simple arithmetic.

- Bob

I got rather different results that were more in line
with what I was expecting relatively for the different
approaches.

I'm running Stan 1.3.0 on R 3.0.0 on a Macbook Pro
with 16GB of memory and an i7 CPU.  I just freshly
installed both because I was behind a revision or two.
I then edited my R Makeconf file here:

   /Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Resources/etc/Makeconf

to set optimization level to -O3 in CFLAGS and CXXFLAGS
lines.  Unlike before, it now says -mtune=core2, which I
left (but I have no idea whether I should have or not).

I also have

  > set_cppo('fast')

set.

I then did two runs, first the script exactly as you sent it,
which used a matrix for the data.

   RUN 1

   matrix[R,C] mat;

   loop over rows of matrix
     user  system elapsed
   83.624   0.306  84.049

   loop in R
     user  system elapsed
   45.188   0.874  47.164

The values are much closer together than you had, with the
looping over data sets a little less than twice as fast.

Then I closed R and restarted it to make sure any comparison
issues weren't due to R's memory management.  Then I did a second
run using an array of row vectors:

    RUN 2

    row_vector[C] mat[R]; // array of vector outcomes

    loop over array of row vectors
       user  system elapsed
    117.639   0.390 117.746

    loop in R
       user  system elapsed
     46.949   0.759  48.942

As I was expecting, the matrix version took about 50% longer
compared to the array of row vectors when accessed by row.

I had noticed that a lot of the time was being spent on
a very slow chain --- chain 3 with the original seed.  So I
just mashed the numberline to generate a new seed

  seed = 9879087987

and got more comparable results:

  loop over array of row vectors
    user  system elapsed
  63.450   0.243  63.476

  loop in R
    user  system elapsed
  45.495   0.875  47.609

I'm really surprised the array of row vectors was slower for
you.

It may be R's memory.  So you might want to try only
running one of these tests per R session.

Do you know which optimization levels you compiled the Stan
libraries and Stan models with?  The default optimization level
is -O2 if you didn't fiddle with it.

To answer the other question, from R help for proc.time:

   The definition of ï¿½userï¿½ and ï¿½systemï¿½ times is from your OS. Typically it is something like
   The ï¿½user timeï¿½ is the CPU time charged for the execution of user instructions of the calling process.
   The ï¿½system timeï¿½ is the CPU time charged for execution by the system on behalf of the calling process.

So it looks like the values can be system dependent.

The doc also says the third column is:

   the ï¿½realï¿½ elapsed time since the process was started

Thanks again for bringing this up.  I'm going to add a discussion
of matrices vs. arrays to the optimization chapter of the manual.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Implementing NUTS in PyMC
messages.body_plain:
The NUTS part itself hasn't changed.

The new code sets everything up as a proper Hamiltonian
involving a mass matrix and a step size (step size = time
interval).  The old code used varying step sizes, which
is similar in effect to a diagonal mass matrix.   It's
important to use a diagonal mass matrix or varying step
sizes.  We haven't evaluated the full matrix enough yet to
have a conclusive answer.

The new code is a bit different in the way it does
adaptation during warmup.  The reason for the change was more
consistency than anything else.

Coming down the road, we're doing RM-HMC and Geometric NUTS.
We have a ways to go with the auto-diff first.

- Bob

Bob:

Thanks - this is all helpful, although puzzling on some points.

Your times indicate that the matrix form is faster than the row_vectors form (like the results we posted yesterday), while your conclusion is that the row_vectors form speeds up the computation. Maybe I'm misinterpreting the proc.time output.
The time we care about is "elapsed time" - time it takes to obtain the results. It is surprising that sometimes the ordering given by elapsed time and by system CPU time are different, and not just by small margins.
The Rstan manual has now omitted changing the makefile to set flags to -O3, and I understood the reason was that using the R command set_cppo("fast") achieved the same optimization in C++ compilation. Does editing Makeconf optimize C++ compilation further than solely using set_cppo("fast")?
Our timing from yesterday was based on R 2.15. We upgraded to R 3.0, and reinstalled STAN and Rstan. This is on a PC with 3.46GB Intel DUO CPU. The new timing is:

         user.self sys.self elapsed
time1    105.50     3.53   109.26     real mat[R,C]                big joint model of independent parameters
time2     37.73   161.17  199.30     real vec[C]                    many individual models via looping in R
time3     68.32     2.80     71.41     row_vector[C] mat[R]     big joint model of independent parameters

So this run exhibits the reduction in timing for row_vectors you originally suggested, about a 35% reduction. What is puzzling about this run is that the looping in R 3.0 now takes 199 for elapsed time instead of 37 in R 2.15.

Given these results, we plan on implementing the hierarchical model with the row_vector data structure.

Thanks for all your work on this issue. Looking forward to your discussion of it in the next version of the manual.

Steve

The first called STAN from R, passed a matrix of 1000x63 to STAN, looped in STAN over i=1,...,1,000 samples (rows), with each sample consisting of 63 observations from a N(mu_i=0, sigma_i=1) distribution (columns), and estimated mu_i and sigma_i. The second approach looped in R over i = 1, ...,1,000 samples and called STAN 1,000 times, once for each sample (row), passing to STAN a vector with 63 observations to estimate mu_i and sigma_i.
>
> The second approach - looping in R - was 20 times as fast as the first approach - looping in STAN.
>
> This is a problem because we plan to use the first approach to implement a hierarchical model on data on 16,000 samples each with 63 observations. Implementing the hierarchical model does not seem possible with the second approach. We are hoping someone can point out why our STAN code for the first approach is inefficient, and what STAN code can be used to achieve the same speed (or better) as the second approach, so that a hierarchical model can be fitted for 16,000 mu_i, sigma_i in reasonable time.
>
> Thanks!
>

>

>  1. Your times indicate that the matrix form is faster than the row_vectors form (like the results we posted yesterday),

>     while your conclusion is that the row_vectors form speeds up the computation. Maybe I'm misinterpreting the

I mislabeled the results --- it was the other way around.
I reran below to make sure.

The array of vectors was faster than matrix.

>  2. The time we care about is "elapsed time" - time it takes to obtain the results. It is surprising that sometimes the

>     ordering given by elapsed time and by system CPU time are different, and not just by small margins.

I think part of the system time may be waiting time for
access to things like file handles, which is going to be
impacted by other things going on in the system.

>  3. The Rstan manual has now omitted changing the makefile to set flags to -O3, and I understood the reason was that

>     using the R command set_cppo("fast") achieved the same optimization in C++ compilation. Does editing Makeconf
>     optimize C++ compilation further than solely using set_cppo("fast")?

I'm still trying to work this out myself.  The key is that
you want to compile the rstan binaries with -O3 optimization.
We'll fix the instructions over the next week to make this
clearer.

> Our timing from yesterday was based on R 2.15. We upgraded to R 3.0, and reinstalled STAN and Rstan. This is on a PC
> with 3.46GB Intel DUO CPU. The new timing is:
>
>           user.self sys.self elapsed
> time1    105.50     3.53   109.26     real mat[R,C]                big joint model of independent parameters
> time2     37.73   161.17  199.30     real vec[C]                    many individual models via looping in R
> time3     68.32     2.80     71.41     row_vector[C] mat[R]     big joint model of independent parameters
>
> So this run exhibits the reduction in timing for row_vectors you originally suggested, about a 35% reduction.

Sorry -- I mislabeled the output, because I'd done them
in the opposite order.  I just reran all the tests to be sure.

Original seed=444
    user  system elapsed
116.242   0.303 116.397  loop over rows of matrix
  81.561   0.274  81.581  loop over array of row vectors
  49.315   0.625  50.781  loop in R

With a different seed, we're actually faster than looping in
R:

New seed=9879087987  (seed = 444 still used in R for data)
    user  system elapsed
  63.034   0.517  63.575    loop over rows of matrix
  46.661   1.034  48.728    loop in R
  44.313   0.188  44.525    loop over array of row vectors

The looping in R is more stably estimated because it's essentially
an average of 1000 independent trials, one for each row.

This also highlights how much variability there is in Stan's
implementation of NUTS and warmup adaptation.  We're in the process
of figuring out how to quantify all the timing and variability issues
across a large number of models.

I think the user time here is measuring the work that's actually
being done by the code locally.  System time's going to include time
to get memory or file handles from the system.  And probbably
process management time.

The other big issue here in profiling is that what we really care
about is effective sample size per second, not number of iterations.
In this case, the two models are equal, so we don't need to adjust
for that, because the samples and hence effective sample sizes should
be the same.

> What is
> puzzling about this run is that the looping in R 3.0 now takes 199 for elapsed time instead of 37 in R 2.15.

I can imagine the system could get bogged down if there
are lots of open file handles or something --- I really don't
know what R does on the back end.  You should try it again with
it the only thing running and other processes shut down.

But this is also one of the reason why it's tough to measure
software performance.  What can work well under low system load
(either file handles, threads, processes, whatever) might not work
well under high system load.  In general, it's better to pool/batch
system requests as much as possible because they tend to be really
slow and scarce compared to executing code.

> Given these results, we plan on implementing the hierarchical model with the row_vector data structure.

That's what I'd recommend.

> Thanks for all your work on this issue. Looking forward to your discussion of it in the next version of the manual.

The next release is going to be a big one.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
To give everyone else some context, the issue (quoting from
Jiqiang's Feb 28 e-mail) is this:

   ## before change
   # Initial values (a function is required)
   radon.inits <- function (){
     list ("a"=a,"b"=b,"mu_a"=mu_a,"sigma_y"=sigma_y,"sigma_a"=sigma_a)
   }

   # after change:
   # Initial values (a function is required)
   radon.inits <- function (){
     list ("a"=a,"b"=array(b, dim = length(b)),"mu_a"=mu_a,"sigma_y"=sigma_y,"sigma_a"=sigma_a)
   }

The problem is R's weak typing and the convention to allow
assignment back and forth.

   > a <- 10
   > aa <- array(a, dim=length(a))

They print the same way:

   > aa
   [1] 10
   > a
   [1] 10

and have the same type:

   > typeof(a)
   [1] "double"
   > typeof(aa)
   [1] "double"

and both are is.double():

   > is.double(a)
   [1] TRUE
   > is.double(aa)
   [1] TRUE

but is.array() can distinguish them:

   > is.array(a)
   [1] FALSE
   > is.array(aa)
   [1] TRUE

but then you can reassign and erase the type again:

   > aa <- a

   > is.array(aa)
   [1] FALSE

Jiqiang --- would it work from the RStan side to just apply this
transform everywhere?

    x   |->  array(x, dim=length(x))

Or will it fail because now it is an array and not a scalar?  I
couldn't even figure out how to test if something's a scalar.
is.double() works for both a and aa.  This should all come down
to the implementation of stan::io::var_context for an R environment.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Specifying parameter/vector dimensions
messages.body_plain:
On Friday, May 17, 2013 5:25:07 PM UTC-4, Jiqiang Guo wrote:
> If I do this
>
> x   |->  array(x, dim=length(x))
>
>
> Bob is right about then I do not know if one is scalar when it is supposed to be.
> Currently, I am assuming vector of length 1 without attributes of "dim"
> being a scalar.  The root reason is that R does not have scalar so there is
> no difference between " a <- 1" and " d <- c(1)".

This definition of scalar includes lists of length 1, which I don't think should be interpret as scalars in the data block of Stan. I would personally define x as a scalar in R with

is.scalar <- function(x) {
  is.vector(x, mode = "any") && !is.list(x) && length(x) == 1
}

Ben

A list of length 1 such as list(3) is equivalent to array(3, dim = c(1, 1)) as we use list
for data declared in Stan as "vector[J] y[I]".

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Error when excuting make bin/libstan.a
messages.body_plain:
My guess, because of where the problem occurred:

    src/stan/agrad/matrix.hpp

that it's a memory issue.  Windows in particular can
have trouble here because their compiler chain is less
memory efficient for some reason.

How much memory do you have?

Also, is this the latest version of Stan (1.3.0)?
And which version of g++ are you using?  Try:

   $ g++ --version

We should figure out how to release binaries, because
once this file's compiled, the rest are easy.  We're also
working on reducing memory requirements during compilation.
But no intermediate releases to try yet.  We're also changing
a bunch of other things and still testing.

- Bob

On our Windows test machine, we are running the g++ distributed by RTools: gcc version 4.6.3 20111208 (prerelease) (GCC)

I just verified that I could run make bin/libstan.a using g++ 4.6.3 and with the default optimization levels.

If you can't change your g++ version, something that might work is playing with the optimization levels. The make variable is O and Stan's default is 3. The other options are 0, 1, 2, and s.

To set it to 0, run:
make bin/libstan.a O=0

You may have to clean in between attempts and to do that, type:
make clean-all

Daniel

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] stand-alone c++ example
messages.body_plain:
On 5/19/13 10:20 PM, a...@ariddell.org wrote:
> Hi,
>
> I'm working towards a python wrapper (using cython). I was wondering if
> there's an example of a simulation written in c++ using only the c++ api
> (i.e., without any intermediate call to an executable like stanc)?

I'm afraid the only example of such a thing is the code generated
by stanc for a model :-)

The model class geneated by stanc handles a number of issues that
are hard to deal with directly, particularly the I/O of

    -- data

    -- initial values (requires transform to unconstrained)

    -- parameter values (requires transform to constrained)

    -- parameter names

    -- samples

The constrained variable declarations get compiled to transforms
that include the differentiable log Jacobian determinant in the
overall log probability function.

The way we wrapped in R was to have the code compile a model class,
then compile it and dynamically link it.  What corresponds to the
main() in the ordinary bin/stanc output is not used and instead,
the class is controlled from R to interface with its memory.

- Bob

> sure they exist). I'll look into the rstan code and see how it gets done with R.

R does have standard tools for both compiling binary
libraries and on-the-fly C++ compilation.

It looks like the weave sub-package of scipy supplies similar
functionality to the inline package we use in R.  All of
our other compilation is done ahead of time.

An alternative to a deep integration is having the
compilation done by system calls.  Our own makefiles
are tested cross-platform.

- Bob

messages.subject: RStan vs. R's glm() function for logistic regression
messages.subject_clean: RStan vs. R's glm() function for logistic regression
messages.body_plain:
I was running some tests for speed, and thought people
might like to see the results.  The bottom line is
that R's glm() function is about 60 times faster than
Stan at fitting a simple logistic regression.

Here's the table, where  K is number of predictors,
and N is the number of dimensions.

The simulated data for predictors and coefficients
were both indepdent unit normal, which is probably
not the most realistic way to set up such a test.
We'll be running some more realistic tests and looking
at hierarchical models vs. R packages lme and blme.

Here's the results:

   K                N    stan()    glm()
                                   time
---------------------------------------------------
  10            1,000       1s      0s
  10           10,000       7s      0s
  10          100,000       1m      2s
  10        1,000,000      10m     20s

  20            1,000       1s      0s
  20           10,000      20s      0s
  20          100,000       2m      2s

  40            1,000      3s       0s
  40           10,000     40s       0s

  80            1,000      6s       0s*
               10,000      1m       1s*

160            1,000      20s      1s*
160           10,000       3m      3s

320            1,000       2m      2s*

640            1,000       9m      8s*

* = convergence issue for glm(), which isn't solved by lowering
     step size or increasing the number of iterations;  whether
     glm() failed often depended on the parameters themselves

Stan will continue to scale, at about the same rate --- I
just got tired waiting for the results and was too lazy
to automate the test process.

Stan runs consist of 200 iterations on 4 chains, all split Rhat < 1.1,
and all parameters > 50 ESS.

glm() run with default settings:

   glm_fit <- glm(y ~ x,family=binomial(link=logit))

Stan model, with prior for beta fixed to the true value:

   data {
     int<lower=1> K;
     int<lower=0> N;
     int<lower=0,upper=1> y[N];
     matrix[N,K] x;
   }
   parameters {
     vector[K] beta;
   }
   model {
     beta ~ normal(0,1);
     y ~ bernoulli_logit(x * beta);
   }

- Bob

On 5/21/13 5:02 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Just out of curiosity, how fast do these compare to running stan in its mode-finding setting?

Good question.  Unfortunately, the answer with the optimizer
currently plugged into RStan 1.3 is 2.3 minutes, which is roughly
the same amount of time as it takes Stan to run NUTS.  Here's
the report:

Iteration  1. Log joint probability =   -3216.52. Improved by 3714.96.
Iteration  2. Log joint probability =   -2083.11. Improved by 1133.4.
Iteration  3. Log joint probability =   -1488.77. Improved by 594.344.
Iteration  4. Log joint probability =   -1187.62. Improved by 301.151.
Iteration  5. Log joint probability =   -1066.97. Improved by 120.65.
Iteration  6. Log joint probability =   -1040.77. Improved by 26.2012.
Iteration  7. Log joint probability =   -1039.23. Improved by 1.53311.
Iteration  8. Log joint probability =   -1039.23. Improved by 0.00638312.
Iteration  9. Log joint probability =   -1039.23. Improved by 1.21573e-07.

The answers match pretty closely for glm(), Stan NUTS, Stan optimization,
and the simulated parameters.

Those last three iterations don't gain us much, especially the last two,
so we could perhaps shave 20% off the optimization time by imposing a less
stringent convergence criterion.

So the comparison for the test I just ran is this:

K               N         Stan NUTS     glm()    Stan optimize
160           10,000       3m            3s         2m

I should also point out that we have a lot of room for
improvement in Stan for these models through writing a custom
logistic_regression() distribution, which would look like.

    y ~ logistic_regression(x,beta);

This will be several times faster than what we do now, but
is unlikely to be 60 times faster.  It'll speed up both optimization
and sampling.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I could e-mail the data, but it's 13MB gzipped.
(10K instances * 160 params = 1.6 million double values)

Or you can generate your own data using the following R code,
which is what I used for the simulations.  Note that there's
an intercept term.  (I also had a line setting beta[2] to -1 for
some reason, but I removed it.)

-------------logistic-sim.R-----------------------

library("rstan");

inv_logit <- function(u) {
   return(1 / (1 + exp(-u)));
}

K <- 160;
N <- 10000;
sigma_beta <- 1;
beta <- rnorm(K,mean=0,sd=sigma_beta);
sigma_x <- 1;
x <- matrix(rnorm(N*K,mean=0,sd=sigma_x),nrow=N,ncol=K);
x[,1] <- rep(1,N);
y <- rep(NA,N);
for (n in 1:N) {
   y[n] <- rbinom(1,1,inv_logit(x[n,] %*% beta));
}

fit <- stan("logistic.stan", data=c("K","N","y","x"), chains=1, iter=2, init=0);

start_time_stanopt <- Sys.time()
ofit <- optimizing(get_stanmodel(fit), data=list(K=K,N=N,y=y,x=x), init=0);
end_time_stanopt <- Sys.time();
elapsed_time_stanopt <- end_time_stanopt - start_time_stanopt;

start_time_glm <- Sys.time()

glm_fit <- glm(y ~ x,family=binomial(link=logit))

end_time_glm <- Sys.time();
elapsed_time_glm <- end_time_glm - start_time_glm;

start_time <- Sys.time()
fit <- stan("logistic.stan", data=c("K","N","y","x"), chains=4, iter=200, init=0, fit=fit);
end_time <- Sys.time();
elapsed_time <- end_time - start_time;
print("");
print("elapsed time, stan():");  print(elapsed_time);
print("elapsed time, glm():");	 print(elapsed_time_glm);

---------------------------------------------------------------------

- Bob

Was that using Newton's method or BFGS? The convergence speed (in
iterations) looks more like Newton (a.k.a. iteratively reweighted
least squares). That Newton implementation is getting the Hessian in a
pretty naive way, which for LR can be much more heavily optimized.

Are we linking against a BLAS? I've been meaning to bring that up as a
possible area for optimization. I would assume that glm is using some
kind of optimized BLAS, which makes a big, big difference when your
primary computational operation is matrix multiplication and
inversion.

Matt

messages.subject: logistic regression with spatial auto-covariate and missing data imputation
messages.subject_clean: logistic regression with spatial auto-covariate and missing data imputation
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm trying to fit a logistic regression to some simulated data, and I'm having trouble retrieving parameter estimates that approximate those that were used to generate the data and was wondering if anyone had any ideas on why this might be.

The model includes a single predictor variable (bounded between 0-1), a spatial auto-covariate, and requires some missing data to be imputed to estimate some of the spatial auto-covariates.

The data was simulated with the following back-story in mind:

The goal of the study is to determine the effect of FPC (foliage projective cover (%)) on distribution of a species in the study area. The square study area was divided up into grid cells of equal sizes.
Observers were sent out to most of the grid cells, and the species was recorded as being present (1) or absent (0) in these grid cells. These observations are assumed to contain no false-positives or false-negatives. However due to finite resources, some grid cells were not visited and the presence or absence of the species in these grid cells is unknown.

This species is known to have a strongly spatially auto-correlated distribution, and so this will be taken into account using a spatial auto-covariate. The spatial-autocovariate for a given cell is the average occupancy in its neighboring cells (max. 8). In order to calculate the spatial auto-covariate for cells that are neighbors with cells that were not visited, the probability of the species occupying the cells that were not visited must be imputed in the model.

I've attached the R script that generates the data, runs my best attempt at the model, and includes my sessionInfo() in the comments (autocovariate_example.txt), the data dump file (autocov_data.txt), and the stan model (autocov_model.txt). The R script is heavily commented so may offer additional context.

Thank you, Jeff

Hi, Jeff.  Just speaking generically, one way to check this sort of fake-data simulation is to draw the parameters from the prior.  Then the posterior coverage should be exact (up to computational accuracy).  For details, you can take a look at the 2006 paper by Cook, Gelman, and Rubin (at my website linked from the published papers page).  It's worth checking, as there can be various reasons (even possibly a Stan bug!) that is causing your problem.
I hope this helps.
Andrew

messages.body_plain:
Did you try building this up from first building a model
without missing data and verifying that it could fit the data?
Then you should have at least the likelihood and priors down.

Also, if you haven't tried it already, I'd also suggest using
some intermediate print statements to make sure all the intermediate
calculations are happening the way you want them to.

(For both of these issues, what we really need is some way to define
and test subprograms in a modular way.)

You might also consider using a Gaussian process logistic regression
model if the number of data points isn't too high --- it seems to have
most of the features you're after built into its basic
structure.

Depending on the kind of problem you're having with fitting,
you might want to choose slightly more informative priors:

   intercept ~ normal(0,1000);
   fpc_slope ~ normal(0,1000);
   auto_slope ~ normal(0,1000);
   sigma_miss ~ gamma(0.001, 0.001);

If the data highly underdetermines a variable with a very fat
prior, it can drag the whole model around with it.  So I'd want
to see what these variables were doing.

As a minor point, I'd define data items like this:

   int numTotalPlus1; // number of grid cells total + 1

as transformed data to make sure they're always right.

If you actually lay the data out
on a grid, you should also be able to calculate quantities
like numNeighbors directly in Stan.

Are statements like these:

       for (currNeighPos in 1:8) {
         currAutoVal<-currAutoVal+Y_total_est[Y_neighMat[missPos[currPos3],currNeighPos]];
       }

appropriately accounting for the edge cases?

Spatially, aren't corner connections different than edge ones?

     A B C
     D . E
     F G H

It seems B/D/E/G should have more effect on the center
than A/C/F/H because of distance.  This is again something the Gaussian
process should do automatically.

- Bob
