messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Implementing NUTS in PyMC
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I continue to have the problem that in my implementation of NUTs the variance of the samples is too high. Would someone mind taking a look at my code?

I literally copy-pasted the algorithm from the paper and tweaked the syntax so it would run as Python, so I would expect it to be easy to understand.

You can find the code and output here: http://nbviewer.ipython.org/urls/raw.github.com/jsalvatier/pymc/79a64fc2d30bfd9d7914498eab19363c9ae91e80/pymc/examples/nuts.ipynb .

I'm also taking a more in depth look at Michael Betancourt's refactoring.

I appreciate any help you can offer :)

John

On Thu, May 16, 2013 at 11:56 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> The NUTS part itself hasn't changed.
>
> The new code sets everything up as a proper Hamiltonian
> involving a mass matrix and a step size (step size = time
> interval).  The old code used varying step sizes, which
> is similar in effect to a diagonal mass matrix.   It's
> important to use a diagonal mass matrix or varying step
> sizes.  We haven't evaluated the full matrix enough yet to
> have a conclusive answer.
>
> The new code is a bit different in the way it does
> adaptation during warmup.  The reason for the change was more
> consistency than anything else.
>
> Coming down the road, we're doing RM-HMC and Geometric NUTS.
> We have a ways to go with the auto-diff first.
>
> - Bob
>
>
>
>

messages.subject: Help with hierarchical model
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I've been using a hierarchical model (model 1 attached) to estimate 23 coefficients based on about 50,000 data points. I have three versions of the model:

Model 1 - first version of the model with observations nested in country. Run for 2000 iterations on 4 chains the model converges with sensible parameter estimates (~2.5 hours).

Model 2 - the same as model 1 but with the 'Matt trick' applied to improve the speed - except it runs more slowly and doesn't quite converge after 2000 iterations. So I guess there is something wrong there.

Model 3 - more complicated model where observations are nested in clusters and clusters nested in countries. So far I have had no success with this version. There are 8000 clusters in the dataset. Some of the clusters only have one observation and there are different numbers of clusters between the countries. It's a lot of parameters to estimate.

Any advice you have on improving the speed in models 2 and 3 would be really great. I am happy I got this far without having to ask a question.

Many thanks,

Sophie

messages.subject: Non-Homogeneous Poisson Process (NHPP) Model
messages.body_plain:
Hi stan-users,

I'm a newcomer to Stan-type models, and I'm wondering if it is possible to implement a Non-Homogeneous Poisson Process (NHPP process model in Stan?  For this exercise I am looking at bugs in software in the NTDS dataset referred to in [goel1997nhpp].

I have been exploring this dataset with grid approximation and I'd like to try it with Stan.

I am using R3.0.1 on Ubuntu and rstan version 1.3.0.

My complete code is:

library(rstan)
# set_cppo("fast")  # for best running speed
set_cppo('debug') # make debug easier

# the failure time in days from the start of testing
bugt <- c(9L, 21L, 32L, 36L, 43L, 45L, 50L, 58L, 63L, 70L, 71L, 77L,
  78L, 87L, 91L, 92L, 95L, 98L, 104L, 105L, 116L, 149L, 156L, 247L,
  249L, 250L, 337L, 384L, 396L, 405L, 540L, 798L, 814L, 849L)

# restrict bugs to the first 26 elements to match the original paper
N <- 26

# visualize the dataset with the mean value function with
# some nominal values
alpha <- 34
beta <- 0.00579
mvt <- function(x) { alpha*(1-exp(-beta*x)) }
curve(mvt, to=250, lty=3, xlab='Time (days)',
      ylab='Cumulative Bugs Found')
points(bugs, 1:26)

bugs_dat <- list(N=N, bugs=bugt[1:N])

# here I try to implement the NHPP model for the NTDS data set
# i.e. Pr{N(t) = y} = Poisson(y, mvt(t)), y=0,1,2,...
# where mvt(t) = alpha*(1-exp(-beta*t))
smodel <- '
  data {
    int<lower=0> N; // number of data points (bugs observed)
    real<lower=0> bugs[N]; // the observed bug times in days
  }
  parameters {
    real<lower=1> alpha; // estimated number of bugs in the system
    real<lower=0> beta;  // finding "rate" parameter
  }
  model {
    for (d in 1:N) {
      bugs[d] ~ poisson(d, alpha*(1-exp(-beta*bugs[d])));
      // lp__ ~ mvt[d]^d*exp(-mvt[d])/d!
    }
  } '

# we expect alpha to be about 34 and beta about 0.00579
# for the first 26 elements of bugt
fit <- stan(model_code = smodel, data = bugs_dat, iter = 1000, chains = 4)

However I'm getting an error:

TRANSLATING MODEL 'smodel' FROM Stan CODE TO C++ CODE NOW.
Error in stanc(file = file, model_code = model_code, model_name = model_name,  :
  failed to parse Stan model 'smodel' with error message:
EXPECTATION FAILURE LOCATION: file=input; line=12, column=7

      bugs[d] ~ poisson(d, alpha*(1-exp(-beta*bugs[d])));
      ^-- here

DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:
no matches for function name="poisson_log"
    arg 0 type=real
    arg 1 type=int
    arg 2 type=real
available function signatures for poisson_log:
0.  poisson_log(int, real) : real
1.  poisson_log(int, real[1]) : real
2.  poisson_log(int, vector) : real
3.  poisson_log(int, row vector) : real
4.  poisson_log(int[1], real) : real
5.  poisson_log(int[1], real[1]) : real
6.  poisson_log(int[1], vector) : real
7.  poisson_log(int[1], row vector) : real
unknown distribution=poisson
Parser expecting: "}"

Is it possible to use such a NHPP model?
Pr{N(t) = y} = Poisson(y, mvt(t)), y=0,1,2,...
where is the mean value function:
 mvt(t) = alpha*(1-exp(-beta*t))

bugs[d] in the model above is the time bug d was detected and alpha is the total expected number of bugs.

Many thanks in advance for your help.

Kind regards,
Seán

@article{goel1997nhpp,
  title={Time-Dependent Error-Detection Rate Model for Software Reliability and Other Performance Measures},
  author={Amrit L. Goel and Kazu Okumoto},
  journal={IEEE Trasactions on Reliability},
  volume={R-28},
  number={3},
  pages={206--211},
  year={1997},
  month={August},
  publisher={IEEE},
  keywords={Software reliability, NHPP, Software modelling, Software failure analysis},
}

--
Kind regards,

Sean O'Riordain
seor...@tcd.ie

messages.subject: Lost in 1093-dimensional space
messages.body_plain:
When reading the 1.3.0 manual for the first time, I was shocked by the ability of stan to handle 1093-dimensional vectors:

For example, a 1093 dimensional row vector u would be declared as row_vector[1093] u; (page 147)

This is far beyond my Einsteinian world is as close to Hilpert-space one can get.

Is there any reason for using "dimensional" here instead of length or size (first part of sentence)?

>From Base R Documentation:

An array in R can have one, two or more dimensions. It is simply a vector which is stored with additional attributes <http://127.0.0.1:25263/help/library/base/help/attributes> giving the dimensions (attribute "dim") and optionally names for those dimensions (attribute "dimnames").

A two-dimensional array is the same thing as a matrix <http://127.0.0.1:25263/help/library/base/help/matrix>.

messages.subject_clean: array/vector/matrix terminology for dimensions vs. size vs. length
messages.body_plain:
Andrew --- you might be the best one to answer this given
our shared love of precise terminology.

On 5/28/13 4:05 AM, Dieter Menne wrote:
> When reading the 1.3.0 manual for the first time, I was shocked by the ability of stan to handle 1093-dimensional vectors:
>
> For example, a 1093 dimensional row vector u would be declared as row_vector[1093] u; (page 147)
>
> This is far beyond my Einsteinian world is as close to Hilpert-space one can get.

I just meant a row vector of size 1093.  Nothing is inherently non-Euclidean.
See below.

> Is there any reason for using "dimensional" here instead of length or size (first part of sentence)?

I was trying to be precise.  The problem with "length" is
that "length" is also used for the L2 norm.  The problem with
size() is that it's non-standard in math, though standard in
C++.

>  From Base R Documentation:
>
> An array in *R* can have one, two or more dimensions. It is simply a vector which is stored with additional attributes
> <http://127.0.0.1:25263/help/library/base/help/attributes> giving the dimensions (attribute |"dim"|) and optionally

> names for those dimensions (attribute |"dimnames"|).
>

> A two-dimensional array is the same thing as a |matrix <http://127.0.0.1:25263/help/library/base/help/matrix>|.

OK --- I see the problem with the terminology here.

Usually if we have [0.9 1.7 -102.789]', that's a vector representing a
point in 3-dimensional space.  0.9 is the first dimension (x),
1.7 the second dimension (y) and -102.789 the third dimension.

But then people talk about "2D array" when they mean it has two
indices.

You can see the overload in the Wikipedia description of arrays
and vectors:

   http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_vector#Other_dimensions

   http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Array_data_structure

I'd like to be consistent and not confuse those used to R, those
used to C++, or those used to mathematical terminology.

But even "vector" is ambiguous between a vector data type and
the mathematical concept of a vector.

I'm thinking we should probably stick to "size" unless someone has
a better suggestion.  But then if I have a 1D array of size
10, how do I refer to the third element of the array?  Maybe "position"?

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Modeling a K-distribution
messages.body_plain:
Thanks Bob and Ben for your feedback on my K-distribution problem! I'm
trying to integrate your comments, will report results later :).

Bob
 proposed to define the likelihood of data y as INT gamma(u|a1,b1) *
gamma(y/u|a2,b2) du. This integral is solveable (see wikipedia on
K-distribution), but leads to a PDF that contains a modified Bessel
function of the second kind which has the form K(alpha,x) = INT[0,Inf]
exp(-x*cosh(t)) * cosh(alpha*t) dt. Not surprisingly, this type of
function is not supported by Stan. I don't even attempt to think what

On Tue, May 28, 2013 at 3:55 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> Andrew --- you might be the best one to answer this given
> our shared love of precise terminology.
>
> On 5/28/13 4:05 AM, Dieter Menne wrote:
> > When reading the 1.3.0 manual for the first time, I was shocked by the ability of stan to handle 1093-dimensional vectors:
> >
> > For example, a 1093 dimensional row vector u would be declared as row_vector[1093] u; (page 147)
> >
> > This is far beyond my Einsteinian world is as close to Hilpert-space one can get.
>
> I just meant a row vector of size 1093.  Nothing is inherently non-Euclidean.
> See below.
>
> > Is there any reason for using "dimensional" here instead of length or size (first part of sentence)?
>
> I was trying to be precise.  The problem with "length" is
> that "length" is also used for the L2 norm.  The problem with
> size() is that it's non-standard in math, though standard in
> C++.
>
> >  From Base R Documentation:
> >
> > An array in *R* can have one, two or more dimensions. It is simply a vector which is stored with additional attributes
> > <http://127.0.0.1:25263/help/library/base/help/attributes> giving the dimensions (attribute |"dim"|) and optionally
> > names for those dimensions (attribute |"dimnames"|).
> >
> > A two-dimensional array is the same thing as a |matrix <http://127.0.0.1:25263/help/library/base/help/matrix>|.
>
> OK --- I see the problem with the terminology here.
>
> Usually if we have [0.9 1.7 -102.789]', that's a vector representing a
> point in 3-dimensional space.  0.9 is the first dimension (x),
> 1.7 the second dimension (y) and -102.789 the third dimension.
>
> But then people talk about "2D array" when they mean it has two
> indices.
>
> You can see the overload in the Wikipedia description of arrays
> and vectors:
>
>   http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_vector#Other_dimensions
>
>   http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Array_data_structure
>
> I'd like to be consistent and not confuse those used to R, those
> used to C++, or those used to mathematical terminology.
>
> But even "vector" is ambiguous between a vector data type and
> the mathematical concept of a vector.
>
> I'm thinking we should probably stick to "size" unless someone has
> a better suggestion.  But then if I have a 1D array of size
> 10, how do I refer to the third element of the array?  Maybe "position"?

>
>
> - Bob

Are you expecting y = L / sigma to have elements

> parameter for the distribution of Z3). As I mentioned before, the uncensored Z3-script works like a charm, whereas the
> censored one gives the problem we are discussing. I put some responses inline below.

> On Friday, 31 May 2013 00:20:44 UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:

>

>

> at least the log_incompl_gamma() function for that. With the latter, you can manually define the log_inv_gamma_cdf().
>
>
>      > 2) The model start adapting, but at a slower and slower pace, until it coming to a grinding halt, freezing R.
>
>     It may just have found a very small step size and be taking a very

>     of iterations.
>
>      > 3) The model flies through the simulations, resulting in effective sample size = 1.
>

>     problem
>      > whatsoever.

>     The usual problem is a variable out of support or a variable
>     without a prior.  I don't see either of those issues in your

>
> My point :). And specifying informative priors (and appropriately constraining the support!) doesn't help either.
>
>
>     Is the X in the model supposed to be the same as the
>     X in the R code to generate data?  If so, I don't
>     understand why it's not:
>
>          X ~ gamma(1/var1,1/var1);
>
>     instead of what you have, which is essentially:

>          X ~ inv_gamma(1/var1, 1/var1);

> Yes absolutely. My bad is that in the model, I should have called this 'X' 'Xinv' instead. I use the inverse of X
> because at some point I have to divide a scalar ('shape#'') by the vector 'X'. To speed things up (which it absolutely
> does!), I therefore model 'Xinv' and multiply this with the scalar. Nifty but perhaps not so handy for the sake of
> comprehension.

It is a tradeoff and Stan's still more like a programming
language than a pure statistical modeling language in that
people will always rewrite models to make them faster.

I like to write out the simpler models, then gradually improve
them for speed.  If you keep the earlier models around, it
provides a guide to others.

You can also add a little doc, but that's often difficult to
do without including so much side commentary that it's distracting.

>     What you'd like to write is:

>          log(gamma_cdf(thres, shape4, shape4 * X[i]));
>

>          log(inv_gamma_cdf(1/thres,shape4,shape4*X[i])
>
> N.B.: If an observation Z is known to be above 'thres', than 1/Z is known to be under 1/thres. The following statement

> corresponds to the log-probability of Z being *above* thres according to the gamma_cdf:
> log*1m*(gamma_cdf(thres, shape4, shape4 * X[i]))

>
> Therefore, the following corresponds to 1/Z being under 1/thres:
> log(inv_gamma_cdf(1/thres,shape4,shape4*X[i])
>
> Conversely, if Z is known to be under thres (1/Z is above 1/thres):

> log*1m*(inv_gamma_cdf(1/thres,shape4,shape4*X[i])

On Friday, May 31, 2013 5:08:52 PM UTC-4, Kevin Bracy Knight wrote:
> I'm really just getting started with Stan and learning as I go here. I have a dataset (attached) of primates and I'm trying to do a multinomial logistic regression. I hijacked the basic code from another user who posted here, and tried to modify it for the purposes of monkeys! The basic idea is that these species are classified based on how endangered they are (from 0 to 4) by a conservation organization. These values are ordinal integers (so categorical classification).

I believe you would want to use an ordered logistic model (section 11.6 of the manual) rather than multinomial logistic model (section 11.5). But the problem of missingness remains. There is some stuff in section 8.1 of the manual, but it is currently pretty difficult to do something good in Stan when there are arbitrary missing data patterns. And it is even more difficult when some of the missing values are discrete.

I would suggest first doing multiple imputation to create m datasets, call stan() once on each of the m datasets, and combine the results using the sflist2stanfit() function in the RStan package.

Ben
